newsitem.title: UK: Currencies worldwide pray for Czech crown reprieve.
newsitem.headline: Currencies worldwide pray for Czech crown reprieve.

text.p: The success or failure of Thai and Czech authorities in defending their bloodied currencies from further speculative attack will have crucial repercussions for currencies across the globe, analysts said on Wednesday.

Thailand appears to have crushed the assault on its baht for now and resisted pressure to devalue. But with the Czech crown's fate still in the balance, danger lurks for the likes of the Slovak crown, South African rand and even the Greek drachma.
"The battle for the Czech National Bank is still very much in the throes and it's not clear which way it's going to go," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS in London.
"If it was forced to devalue there would be other currencies within eastern Europe which would likely be targeted -- the most obvious being the Slovak crown."
Last week the Czech central bank had jacked up a key interest rate to 50 percent from 14 percent after its currency had slipped more than five percent below a basket of dollars and marks.

Market concern over bloated current account deficits has sparked hefty speculative selling of the Czech and Thai units, prompting official intervention, interest rate hikes and -- in the Thai case -- a central bank move to forbid commercial banks from offering short-term baht funds to foreign buyers.
The diminishing pressure on the baht means currencies like the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso can breathe easier.

"If one had gone (devalued) they'd have all gone last week, one after the other. The contagion effect has been seen off, for the time being at least," said Nick Douch, economic and corporate risk adviser at BZW here.
A Thai devaluation would have turned up the heat, especially on a currency like the South African rand, Douch believed.

"South Africa doesn't have the reserves that the other countries have, and it would be difficult for them to put rates up much further because of the nature of the economy -- it's much more open than some of the others," he said.

The Czech crown's troubles, meantime, have turned the spotlight on its eastern European neighbours. The Slovak crown is in the direct firing line as Slovakia too has a current account deficit -- plus political uncertainty, analysts said.
But Philip Poll, director of research at ING Barings, said each market had to be examined on its individual merits.

"There is always a potential risk of contamination as the same investors are targeting those markets," said Poll. "But we would not be concerned of contamination for other currencies (in the region). The fundamentals don't justify that for Poland, Russia or Romania."

Analysts said the rouble should be safe as Russia enjoys a current account surplus and growing foreign exchange reserves, while Romania, Ukraine and Bulgaria appeal to foreign investors as they are seen as exciting new markets offering high yields.

"People investing in the Czech crown are not the same investor class as those investing in Russia or Romania," said Eric Fine, vice-president at Morgan Stanley, noting that the Czech Republic has an investment grade credit rating.

Poland and Hungary may be geographically close to the Czech Republic, but different fiscal policies and trade balances should protect their currencies -- though analysts said any Czech devaluation could provoke cross-border ripples as the crown became more competitive.

"Depending on the size of the devaluation, that would shift the terms of trade within the region, so that may increase pressure on some of the other currencies which appear to be in good shape, such as the zloty and forint," said UBS' Lambert.

Even Greece -- ensconced as it is in the European Union and committed to monetary union -- is potentially at risk, thanks to substantial real appreciation of the drachma and deterioration of external accounts, Lambert said. Thailand's example, however, offers comfort to countries afraid they may be the next target of voracious speculators.
"If the Thais had been forced into a devaluation I think you'd have seen a series of these attacks, because people would use profits to move onto the next target," said BZW's Douch.
"Now they're having to use losses. There's quite a lot of blood around."
